title: Ionic bonding and lattices
keyIdea: When a metal reacts with a non-metal, electrons transfer from the metal atoms to the non-metal atoms, making positive and negative ions. Ionic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions. The ions form a giant lattice in which each ion attracts all its neighbours, so ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct only when melted or dissolved.
familyTip: Look at table salt with a magnifying glass: the tiny cubes come from the cube-shaped lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Ask why salt water can carry a current in a circuit but dry salt crystals cannot, and why salt does not melt in a hot pan.

visual.caption: Does it conduct electricity? Drag each sample into a box, or tap the sample then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: move an electron from Na to Cl, see an ion pulled in every direction, build a lattice, count MgCl₂, melt salt and test conduction.

kid: A sodium atom has one electron in its outer shell (2,8,1). A chlorine atom has seven (2,8,7). When they react, sodium gives its outer electron to chlorine. Sodium becomes Na⁺ and chlorine becomes Cl⁻. Both now have a full outer shell.

Opposite charges attract. The ionic bond is this strong pull between positive and negative ions. Each ion pulls on every ion of the other charge around it, not just one partner. So salt is not made of NaCl molecules. It is a giant lattice of ions packed in a regular pattern.
The formula shows the ratio of ions, and the charges must add to zero. Magnesium makes Mg²⁺, so it needs two Cl⁻ ions: MgCl₂. With O²⁻ the charges already cancel, so magnesium oxide is MgO.

Breaking the lattice means pulling apart many strong attractions, so a lot of energy is needed. Salt melts at 801 °C. Solid salt does not conduct, because its ions are fixed. When it is melted or dissolved in water, the ions can move and carry charge, so it conducts.
adult: Ages 14 to 16. AQA GCSE Chemistry 4.2.1.2 and 4.2.1.3. When a metal reacts with a non-metal, the metal atoms lose their outer electrons and the non-metal atoms gain them. Both ions end up with the electron structure of a noble gas. An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions. Strong electrostatic forces hold it together, and they act in all directions.

Spec point 4.2.2.3: ionic compounds have high melting points. They conduct when melted or dissolved, because then the ions can move. In sodium chloride each ion has six neighbours of the other charge. The lab shows a flat slice, so each inner ion has four. The formula comes from the ratio that makes the total charge zero: NaCl, MgCl₂, MgO. Bigger charges pull harder, so MgO melts at about 2850 °C and NaCl at 801 °C.

Common mistakes: calling ionic compounds molecules or ion pairs; saying electrons are shared, which is covalent bonding; giving the metal a negative charge because it lost something; writing formulas that do not balance, such as MgCl; saying the bonds are weak; and thinking solid salt conducts because it has ions, or that free electrons carry the current in a melt.

In the lab students drag sodium's outer electron to chlorine and tap an ion to see every pull on it. They build a 3 by 3 lattice where like charges repel, count ions in magnesium chloride, heat salt past 801 °C and test solid, molten and dissolved salt in a circuit.

practice.prompt: What happens to electrons when sodium reacts with chlorine?
choices: Sodium transfers one electron to chlorine
Sodium and chlorine share a pair of electrons
Chlorine transfers one electron to sodium
practice.hint: Metals lose outer electrons; non-metals gain them.
practice.explain: Sodium (2,8,1) loses its outer electron to chlorine (2,8,7), giving Na⁺ (2,8) and Cl⁻ (2,8,8). Sharing is covalent bonding.

practice.prompt: Which statement best describes the structure of sodium chloride?
choices: A giant lattice of oppositely charged ions
A lattice of atoms sharing electrons
practice.hint: Does each ion belong to one partner, or to all its neighbours?
practice.explain: Each ion is attracted to every oppositely charged ion around it, so the compound is a giant ionic lattice with no separate molecules.

practice.prompt: A crystal of magnesium oxide contains {n} Mg²⁺ ions. How many O²⁻ ions does it contain?
practice.hint: Compare the sizes of the charges: 2+ and 2−.
practice.explain: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ cancel one to one (MgO), so {n} Mg²⁺ ions come with {n} O²⁻ ions.

practice.prompt: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity?
choices: Its ions are fixed in the lattice
practice.hint: A current needs charged particles that can move.
practice.explain: Solid NaCl is made of ions, but they are held in fixed positions. Melted or dissolved, the ions can move, so it conducts.

practice.prompt: A lattice sample contains {n} Mg²⁺ ions. How many Cl⁻ ions does it contain?
practice.hint: Magnesium chloride is MgCl₂: two Cl⁻ for every Mg²⁺.
practice.explain: The ratio is 1 : 2, so {n} Mg²⁺ ions come with {=2*n} Cl⁻ ions, and the charges cancel: +{=2*n} and −{=2*n}.

pool.prompt: What is the formula of calcium chloride (Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻)?
pool.hint: Balance the charges so they add to zero.
pool.explain: One Ca²⁺ (2+) is balanced by two Cl⁻ (1− each), so the formula is CaCl₂.

pool.prompt: What is the formula of magnesium oxide (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻)?
pool.hint: The two charges are the same size.
pool.explain: 2+ and 2− cancel in a 1 : 1 ratio, so the formula is MgO.

pool.prompt: Why does sodium chloride have a high melting point?
choices: Many strong electrostatic attractions must be overcome
Its covalent bonds are hard to break
pool.hint: What holds the lattice together, and in how many directions?
pool.explain: Strong attractions act between oppositely charged ions in all directions through the giant lattice, so a lot of energy is needed to melt it (801 °C).

pool.prompt: What carries the current in molten sodium chloride?
pool.hint: Ionic compounds have no delocalised electrons.
pool.explain: When it melts, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are free to move and carry charge. There are no free electrons in an ionic compound.

pool.prompt: Why does magnesium oxide melt at a much higher temperature than sodium chloride?
choices: Its ions have larger charges, so the attractions are stronger
pool.explain: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double the charges of Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the electrostatic attractions are much stronger and more energy is needed.

pool.prompt: Aluminium forms Al³⁺ ions. How many Cl⁻ ions balance {n} Al³⁺ ions?
pool.hint: Each Al³⁺ needs three Cl⁻ so the charges add to zero (AlCl₃).
pool.explain: {n} Al³⁺ ions carry +{=3*n}, so {=3*n} Cl⁻ ions are needed to cancel it.

pool.prompt: A sample of sodium chloride contains {n} Na⁺ ions. How many ions does it contain in total?
pool.hint: NaCl has one Cl⁻ for every Na⁺.
pool.explain: {n} Na⁺ and {n} Cl⁻ make {=2*n} ions in total.

pool.prompt: In the sodium chloride crystal, how many Cl⁻ ions surround each Na⁺ ion?
pool.hint: Think of the 3-D cube: up, down, left, right, front and back.
pool.explain: Each Na⁺ has six Cl⁻ neighbours (and each Cl⁻ six Na⁺), which is why there are no separate NaCl molecules.

pool.prompt: Which electronic structure does a Na⁺ ion have?
pool.hint: Sodium is 2,8,1 and loses one electron.
pool.explain: Losing the single outer electron leaves 2,8, the same electronic structure as neon.

pool.prompt: Potassium chloride dissolves in water. Does the solution conduct?
choices: Only if it is heated to 801 °C
pool.hint: What happens to the lattice when it dissolves?
pool.explain: Dissolving frees the K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, so they can move and carry a current.
